title: Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary
text:
Ocean Sound Conditions


Soundscapes vary across years, seasons, and even within a day. Differences are driven by shifts in wind and weather patterns, migration and behavior of animals, and patterns in human activities. We track how sound levels change in different frequencies using standardized soundscape metrics to understand these changes. Seasonal and annual percentiles of all the data are used to define typical conditions.



What are the seasonal patterns across frequencies?


Season is often a main driver of soundscape differences: wind and weather patterns shift, species migrate or change behavior, and humans change their marine activities. As shown on the graphic(s) below, we can visualize the differences by looking at the variation across frequency (pitch of the sound in Hertz) shown on the x-axis and intensity (how loud the sound is in decibels) shown on the y-axis. The colored lines represent seasonal categories, vertical lines are the start of a frequency range that continues over the shaded area that a sound source of interest can be heard, and the black lines bound the soundscape to expected range of intensity based on when only wind noiseis present.
 
 Here are some questions to consider when viewing the graph(s) below: 
 
 (1) Which season has the highest sound levels?
 
 (2) Are there peaks in the sound levels for any of the sounds of interest?
 
 (3) Are the low-frequency sound levels outside the expected range for wind noise?




How are ocean sound conditions changing across years?


Comparing annual ocean sound levels over time can track changes in ocean noise and its contributors. Efforts to reduce noise impacts to marine animals are underway on local to global scales. Strategies can include avoidance of times and areas with high vulnerability, changing the operation of a noise source (e.g., by slowing down) or through the design and use of alternative, quieter sources (vessel speed reduction strategies. The effectiveness of these approaches, and the scales over which they are effective, can be tracked through comprehensive monitoring efforts. A focused analysis is often necessary to tease apart the multiple drivers of ocean sound levels, however, annual summaries provide initial insights to overall patterns.

 Here are some questions to consider when viewing the graph(s) below: 

 (1) Are levels lower in the most recent year of monitoring in any of the frequencies of interest?

(2) Are there peaks in the sound levels for any of the sounds of interest? Do they differ across years?



                    
    




How often are sources of interest likely present?


When sound levels deviate from expected based on wind speed and depth of the monitoring site, other sources are likely present in the soundscape. While this metric does not distinguish between types of sources (e.g. vocalizing species or human activity), it does indicate what percent of the time the soundscape contains sounds of interest to resource managers. When shifts in this metric are observed, further analysis is recommended to understand what is driving the shifts in patterns. For example, are species shifting the timing of their presence in the area? 



                    
    




Are sounds of interest within typical range?


In some soundscapes, we can use specific frequencies as indicators for the presence of a source of interest (e.g. species presence and behavior). Monitoring sites are often chosen because a known source is present and we want to track that source. These sources need to be the dominant sound energy contributor to the specific frequency or frequency range. For example, seasonal migration of humpback whales to Hawaiian Islands results in soundscapes dominated by their calling. At sites near commercial shipping lanes, 63 Hz and 125 Hz are used as an indicator for ship noise. Only frequencies that have been identified as reliable for tracking a source of interest are shown below.

title: Publishing
text:
To get your Quarto webpage to show up with the url
you have a few steps.

title: Publishing
section: Turn on GitHub Pages for your repo
text:
Turn on GitHub Pages for your repo

Turn on GitHub Pages under Settings > Pages . You will set pages to be made from the gh-pages branch and the root directory.
Turn on GitHub Actions under Settings > Actions > General

The GitHub Action will automatically recreate your website when you push to GitHub after you do the initial gh-pages set-up

title: Publishing
section: Do your first publish to gh-pages
text:
Do your first publish to gh-pages
The first time you publish to gh-pages, you need to do so locally.

On your local computer, open a terminal window and cd to your repo directory. Here is what that cd command looks like for me. You command will look different because your local repo will be somewhere else on your computer.

cd ~/Documents/GitHub/NOAA-quarto-simple

Publish to the gh-pages. In the terminal type

quarto publish gh-pages
This is going to render your webpage and then push the _site contents to the gh-pages branch.

title: Publishing
text:
Don’t like using gh-pages?
In some cases, you don’t want your website on the gh-pages branch. For example, if you are creating releases and you want the website pages archived in that release, then you won’t want your website pages on the gh-pages branch.
Here are the changes you need to make if you to avoid gh-pages branch.

At the top of _quarto.yml add the following:

project: 
  type: website
  output-dir: docs

On GitHub under Settings > Pages set pages to be made from the main branch and the docs directory.
Make sure docs is not listed in .gitignore
Publish the site the first time locally using quarto publish from the terminal
Change the GitHub Action because you can’t use quarto publish gh-pages. You’ll need to push to the main branch yourself (in the GitHub Action)

on:
  push:
    branches: main

name: Render and Publish

jobs:
  build-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    steps:
      - name: Check out repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v2 
        
      - name: Set up R (needed for Rmd)
        uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2

      - name: Install packages (needed for Rmd)
        run: Rscript -e 'install.packages(c("rmarkdown", "knitr", "jsonlite"))'

      - name: Set up Quarto
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2
        with:
          # To install LaTeX to build PDF book 
          # tinytex: true 
          # uncomment below and fill to pin a version
          # version: 0.9.600
      
      - name: Render Quarto Project
        uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/render@v2
        with:
          to: html

      - name: Set up Git
        run: |
          git config --local user.email "actions@github.com"
          git config --local user.name "GitHub Actions"

      - name: Commit all changes and push
        run: |
          git add -A && git commit -m 'Build site' || echo "No changes to commit"
          git push origin || echo "No changes to commit"

title: Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary Soundscape Report
text:
Ocean sound monitoring in Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary (OCNMS) and surrounding region has a long history, including efforts by the U.S. Navy and the NOAA Northwest Fisheries Science Center, who have maintained national security and protected endangered species like the Southern Resident Killer Whales. Extensive co-located acoustic telemetry sensors track important prey species, like salmon, and complements underwater sound recordings to more fully characterize the OCNMS ecosystems. 

A Noise Reference Station was added to this region in 2014 and continues to provide long-term monitoring of offshore areas of the western sanctuary. Additionally, in 2019 sanctuaries began monitoring sanctuary soundscapes, as part of the Sanctuary Soundscape Monitoring Project, in four locations and currently maintains one of those stations critical for tracking the status and trends of cetaceans and ship noise on the U.S.-Canadian border, inside major shipping lanes at Swiftsure Bank. 

Current ONMS ocean sound monitoring and analysis is is maintained at two sites. At OC02 vessel traffic and whale activity dominate the soundscape in this area which is the middle of major shipping lanes on the international border, adjacent to a military testing range and inside humpback whale critical habitat known as "Swiftsure Bank". And, the Noise Reference Station site (NRS03) is a deep water site that captures large whale and orca activity offshore and is to the west of the traffic zones for commercial vessels transiting in/out of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. It monitors the northwestern area of the sanctuary, including for Naval testing and training activity.

How much noise from large vessels may be interfering with whale communication?


Sound levels rise when ships are transiting in an area due to engine and propeller noise. The elevated noise interferes with biological communication in the same frequencies. We used a monthly metric to assess noise interference. Ocean sound data was combined with ship tracking data. Nearby ship presence is tracked using data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), an onboard transponder that  most ships are required to use to transmit their location and identity. Ship traffic can vary and this may influence the level of noise in the environment. Periods with different numbers of ships transiting nearby were compared to understand the difference: no ships, low number of ships ( less than 3), medium number of ships (3 to 5 ships ), and high number of ships (more than 5).

text:
Ocean Sound Conditions


Soundscapes vary across years, seasons, and even within a day. Differences are driven by shifts in wind and weather patterns, migration and behavior of animals, and patterns in human activities. We track how sound levels change in different frequencies using standardized soundscape metrics to understand these changes. Seasonal and annual percentiles of all the data are used to define typical conditions.



What are the seasonal patterns across frequencies?


Season is often a main driver of soundscape differences: wind and weather patterns shift, species migrate or change behavior, and humans change their marine activities. As shown on the graphic(s) below, we can visualize the differences by looking at the variation across frequency (pitch of the sound in Hertz) shown on the x-axis and intensity (how loud the sound is in decibels) shown on the y-axis. The colored lines represent seasonal categories, vertical lines are the start of a frequency range that continues over the shaded area that a sound source of interest can be heard, and the black lines bound the soundscape to expected range of intensity based on when only wind noiseis present.
 
 Here are some questions to consider when viewing the graph(s) below: 
 
 (1) Which season has the highest sound levels?
 
 (2) Are there peaks in the sound levels for any of the sounds of interest?
 
 (3) Are the low-frequency sound levels outside the expected range for wind noise?




How are ocean sound conditions changing across years?


Comparing annual ocean sound levels over time can track changes in ocean noise and its contributors. Efforts to reduce noise impacts to marine animals are underway on local to global scales. Strategies can include avoidance of times and areas with high vulnerability, changing the operation of a noise source (e.g., by slowing down) or through the design and use of alternative, quieter sources (vessel speed reduction strategies. The effectiveness of these approaches, and the scales over which they are effective, can be tracked through comprehensive monitoring efforts. A focused analysis is often necessary to tease apart the multiple drivers of ocean sound levels, however, annual summaries provide initial insights to overall patterns.

 Here are some questions to consider when viewing the graph(s) below: 

 (1) Are levels lower in the most recent year of monitoring in any of the frequencies of interest?

(2) Are there peaks in the sound levels for any of the sounds of interest? Do they differ across years?



                    
    




How often are sources of interest likely present?


When sound levels deviate from expected based on wind speed and depth of the monitoring site, other sources are likely present in the soundscape. While this metric does not distinguish between types of sources (e.g. vocalizing species or human activity), it does indicate what percent of the time the soundscape contains sounds of interest to resource managers. When shifts in this metric are observed, further analysis is recommended to understand what is driving the shifts in patterns. For example, are species shifting the timing of their presence in the area? 



                    
    




Are sounds of interest within typical range?


In some soundscapes, we can use specific frequencies as indicators for the presence of a source of interest (e.g. species presence and behavior). Monitoring sites are often chosen because a known source is present and we want to track that source. These sources need to be the dominant sound energy contributor to the specific frequency or frequency range. For example, seasonal migration of humpback whales to Hawaiian Islands results in soundscapes dominated by their calling. At sites near commercial shipping lanes, 63 Hz and 125 Hz are used as an indicator for ship noise. title: Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary Soundscape Report
text:
Ocean sound monitoring in Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary (MBNMS) coordinated by ONMS began in 2018 through the Sanctuary Soundscape Monitoring Project. This sanctuary has a long history of underwater acoustic monitoring dating back to measurements in the 1950s by the U.S. Navy near Point Sur Ridge. The Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) supports a continuous real-time monitoring effort within the sanctuary that began in 2015, known as the Soundscape Listening Room. Collectively, these underwater sound monitoring efforts have provided key insights on cryptic species, whale migration patterns and drivers, methods for detecting fish sounds, and steady rise in ocean noise levels, to highlight a few.

Current ONMS ocean sound monitoring and analysis is maintained at four locations in the sanctuary, as well MBARI hydrophone. These four sites capture unique soundscapes. MB01 is in the middle of Monterey Bay, and on the edge of Monterey Canyon, is busy with foraging animals and vessels for commercial and recreational activities including fishing, whale watching and occasional visits from large cruise ships. MB02 is adjacent to four marine protected areas and in rich kelp forest habitat, this shallow area off Point Pinos has a lot of vessel traffic in and out of Monterey Harbor. MB03 is offshore in the middle of transit lanes for ships weighing 300+ gross tons, this is a deep water area teeming with wide-ranging marine mammals, such as whales and dolphins. This site has decades of broadband sound data in its time-series and is managed by our partners at the Naval Postgraduate School. MB05 is located in La Cruz canyon, part of the understudied Big Sur coast, and recognized as an area of special ecological significance just inside the southern boundary of the Monterey Bay sanctuary. This is the only California site where we hear bocaccio rockfish chorusing year round, and is an important blue whale observatory. This site is also adjacent to the Morro Bay wind energy development area.

Overview of ocean sound monitoring effort


NOAA's Office of National Marine Sanctuaries (ONMS) maintains a nationally coordinated underwater sound monitoring network across the National Marine Sanctuary System, known as ONMS Sound. Recordings and standardized sound measurements are available through the NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information's (NCEI) Passive Acoustic Archive. text:
Understanding ocean sound


Soundscapes are complex – representing a variety of sounds from different sources present at a given time and location, and influenced by the weather. Each sanctuary has unique soundscapes or combinations of sounds present at any given time. We can track soundscape conditions over time and across sites using standardized soundscape metrics. We can also use ocean sound data as indicators for different sources in a soundscape (whales or vessels).  





                    
    


Image: Aline Design for NOAA



Ocean Sound Conditions


Soundscapes vary across years, seasons, and within a day. Differences are driven by shifts in wind and weather patterns, migration and behavior of animals, and patterns in human activities. To compare differences we track how sound levels change in different frequencies using standardized soundscape metrics.  Seasonal and annual percentiles of all the data are used to see how daily values fall within ranges for a given monitoring location.  The example graphic below shows how we visualize soundscape conditions within different seasonal categories. 

Sound is measured in terms of frequency (pitch of the sound in Hertz) shown on the x-axis and intensity (how loud the sound is in decibels) shown on the y-axis. The colored lines represent seasonal categories, vertical lines are the start of a frequency range that continues over the shaded area that a sound source of interest can be heard, and the black lines bound the soundscape to expected range of intensity based on when only wind noise is present.



                    
    




Ocean Sound Indicators


Ocean sound indicators are resource management-relevant metrics derived from long-term monitoring of ocean sound. These indicators track the status and trend of habitat condition, species presence, human-use patterns, and management activities. There are many analytical methods used to generate ocean sound indicators. In some locations sound frequencies are dominated by a specific source and we can use this frequency (e.g. 125 Hz for vessel noise) to track conditions. Other methods detect specific sources of interest. For example, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) maintains analysis of presence of marine mammals from ocean sound monitoring data. text:
Cordell Bank National Marine Sanctuary (CBNMS) sits offshore of California, near San Francisco. CBNMS is bordered by Greater Farallones National Marine Sanctuary (CGNMF) which extends north, south, and towards the coastline. The monitoring location is part of a national soundscape monitoring program, the Noise Reference Station (NRS) Network, which is a collaborative effort with ONMS, the National Marine Fisheries Service, the National Park Service, and the Pacific Marine Environmental Laboratory. The instrument is suspended in deep water (~550m) to maximize the listening range of the hydrophone for low-frequency sounds generated within sanctuary waters.  Baseline soundscape conditions from the first years of sampling (2015-2017) described seasonal baleen whale presence and ongoing vessel noise propagating from the shipping lanes leading to San Francisco and Oakland.
 Monitoring continues at this location to capture sound associated with vessel traffic coming in/out of the Ports of San Francisco and Oakland to the south and west. It's also an area with high baleen whale occurrence seasonally.

Ocean Sound Conditions


Soundscapes vary across years, seasons, and even within a day. Differences are driven by shifts in wind and weather patterns, migration and behavior of animals, and patterns in human activities. We track how sound levels change in different frequencies using standardized soundscape metrics to understand these changes. Seasonal and annual percentiles of all the data are used to define typical conditions.



What are the seasonal patterns across frequencies?


Season is often a main driver of soundscape differences: wind and weather patterns shift, species migrate or change behavior, and humans change their marine activities. As shown on the graphic(s) below, we can visualize the differences by looking at the variation across frequency (pitch of the sound in Hertz) shown on the x-axis and intensity (how loud the sound is in decibels) shown on the y-axis. The colored lines represent seasonal categories, vertical lines are the start of a frequency range that continues over the shaded area that a sound source of interest can be heard, and the black lines bound the soundscape to expected range of intensity based on when only wind noiseis present.
 
 Here are some questions to consider when viewing the graph(s) below: 
 
 (1) Which season has the highest sound levels?
 
 (2) Are there peaks in the sound levels for any of the sounds of interest?
 
 (3) Are the low-frequency sound levels outside the expected range for wind noise?



                    
    



                How was this calculated?
            
                Processing audio to calibrated sound levels (aka soundscape metrics) involves multiple steps to get a specified time frequency data product. All comparisons in the ONMS soundscape inventory reports are hourly power spectral densities in 1 Hz for each third-octave band center frequency. Data processed during the Sanctuary Soundscape Project (pre- 2022 ONMS Sound data) used the Triton Soundscape Remora and data processed for the ONMS sound used either MANTA or PyPAM . Both processing softwares calculated power spectral density (PSD) levels as the median of mean-square pressure amplitude (μPa2). Triton outputs a resolution of 1 Hz/1-sec. MANTA and PyPAM outputs a resolution of hybrid milli-decidade per second. Triton uses 0% overlap in spectral decompositions and MANTA/PyPAM uses 50% overlap, resulting in slight differences in values between these processing softwares. Triton then calculated PSD levels per hour as the median of mean-square pressure amplitude (μPa2) with a resolution of 1 Hz from 20 Hz to 24,000 Hz over no less than 1800 seconds in each hour and converted to decibels (dB re 1 μPa2/Hz). Third-octave band sound pressure levels (TOLs) then were calculated by integration of PSD levels over each octave band with nominal center frequencies. MANTA and PyPAM do the same calculation as Triton to get PSD levels from 1 Hz/1 sec PSDs to hourly but at a 1-minute resolution and within the hybrid millie-decide bands. This difference in time averaging impacts the comparability of the results, and caution should be used when reviewing results that include SanctSound Triton generated hourly data (e.g. TOL_1h.csv). Compatibility between PyPAM and Manata were verified.
 
For the MANTA and PyPAM results PAMscapes was used to calculate one-third octave bands (using createOctaveLevel(hmdData, type='tol') and then the median for each hour with binSoundscapeData(cDataTOL, bin = "1hour", method = c("median")). Hourly data were then matched with an estimate of wind speed at that location using matchGFS in PAMscapes (Global Forecast System (GFS) weather model). Hourly TOLs were then converted back to 1-Hz resolution to match the wind model results (dB re 1 μPa/Hz).  







                
                    Close
                
            
                
                    How does my sanctuary compare?
                
            
                How do soundscape conditions compare across sites? We can use other monitoring sites in similar oceanographic settings (e.g. coastal or offshore) to visualize differences. Data collected across sites during a dedicated monitoring period, like the Sanctuary SoundScape Monitoring Project, can provide initial insights on the differences. In this visualization, soundscape conditions across multiple sites are shown in a specific month, and the black curve represents the site in this sanctuary. What is different? What is the same?  To understand drivers of these differences, this study provides initial insights on how soundscapes compare across ONMS.
                
                    Close
                
            




How are ocean sound conditions changing across years?


Comparing annual ocean sound levels over time can track changes in ocean noise and its contributors. Efforts to reduce noise impacts to marine animals are underway on local to global scales. Strategies can include avoidance of times and areas with high vulnerability, changing the operation of a noise source (e.g., by slowing down) or through the design and use of alternative, quieter sources (vessel speed reduction strategies. The effectiveness of these approaches, and the scales over which they are effective, can be tracked through comprehensive monitoring efforts. A focused analysis is often necessary to tease apart the multiple drivers of ocean sound levels, however, annual summaries provide initial insights to overall patterns.

 Here are some questions to consider when viewing the graph(s) below: 

 (1) Are levels lower in the most recent year of monitoring in any of the frequencies of interest?

(2) Are there peaks in the sound levels for any of the sounds of interest? Do they differ across years?



                    
    




How often are sources of interest likely present?


When sound levels deviate from expected based on wind speed and depth of the monitoring site, other sources are likely present in the soundscape. While this metric does not distinguish between types of sources (e.g. vocalizing species or human activity), it does indicate what percent of the time the soundscape contains sounds of interest to resource managers. When shifts in this metric are observed, further analysis is recommended to understand what is driving the shifts in patterns. For example, are species shifting the timing of their presence in the area? 



                    
    




Are sounds of interest within typical range?


In some soundscapes, we can use specific frequencies as indicators for the presence of a source of interest (e.g. species presence and behavior). Monitoring sites are often chosen because a known source is present and we want to track that source. These sources need to be the dominant sound energy contributor to the specific frequency or frequency range. For example, seasonal migration of humpback whales to Hawaiian Islands results in soundscapes dominated by their calling. At sites near commercial shipping lanes, 63 Hz and 125 Hz are used as an indicator for ship noise. Only frequencies that have been identified as reliable for tracking a source of interest are shown below.

Ocean Sound Indicators


We can use long-term monitoring of ocean sound to derive and track indicators of ocean conditions. These indicators track the status and trend of habitat condition, species presence, human-use patterns, and management activities.  There are many analytical methods used to generate ocean sound indicators. Below are ocean sound indicators relevant to the sanctuary and available for  condition tracking. 



What are the trends in ocean noise?


The purpose of the Ocean Noise Reference Station network is to track trends in low-frequency ocean noise. Year-1 of monitoring was used as a reference point. The monthly median sound levels during the reference year were calculated for the low-frequency sound environment, specifically 63 and 125 Hz. Changes from the reference year are presented as (1) the difference in decibels from reference monthly median values (positive means louder, negative means quieter), and (2) time above the reference monthly median by comparing the hourly values to the  reference value and tallying for how much of the time is above. 




How much noise from large vessels may be interfering with whale communication?


Sound levels rise when ships are transiting in an area due to engine and propeller noise. The elevated noise interferes with biological communication in the same frequencies. We used a monthly metric to assess noise interference. Ocean sound data was combined with ship tracking data. Nearby ship presence is tracked using data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), an onboard transponder that  most ships are required to use to transmit their location and identity. Higher median values indicate more interference with biological communication at the specified frequency. 



How does the level of traffic change conditions?


Ship traffic can vary and this may influence the level of noise in the environment. Periods with different numbers of ships transiting nearby were compared to understand the difference: no ships, low number of ships ( less than 3), medium number of ships (3 to 5 ships ), and high number of ships (more than 5).

title: Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary Soundscape Report
text:
Ocean sound monitoring within Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary (SBNMS) has a long history with a focus on monitoring marine mammals, fishes and vessel noise to inform the status and trends of human activities and marine mammals. Multiple sites in the sanctuary were part of the Sanctuary Soundscape Monitoring Project, a 5-year (2018 to 2022) system-wide monitoring project to understand the diversity of sounds in sanctuary waters. 

Ocean sound monitoring and analysis is maintained at three sites within SBNMS. Two sites (SB01, SB03) capture vessel activity and sounds in higher use areas of the sanctuary. A third site (NRS09) captures migrating whale patterns and vessel traffic in an area closed to some activities, and is part of the U.S. Ocean Noise Reference Station Network.

Current ONMS ocean sound monitoring and analysis is maintained at three sites. SB01 is a historical monitoring site that supports seasonally high abundances of Atlantic cod and is located near a region of elevated commercial vessel activity. SB03 is a shallow sandy habitat situated on the bank that supports the foraging and social activities of marine mammals. And, the Noise Reference Station site (NRS09) has a long term low frequency recording with more propagation exposure to longer distance sounds and in a place protected from fishing, known as a Dedicated Habitat Research Area.

                Processing audio to calibrated sound levels (aka soundscape metrics) involves multiple steps to get a specified time frequency data product. MANTA and PyPAM do the same calculation as Triton to get PSD levels from 1 Hz/1 sec PSDs to hourly but at a 1-minute resolution and within the hybrid millie-decide bands. This difference in time averaging impacts the comparability of the results, and caution should be used when reviewing results that include SanctSound Triton generated hourly data (e.g. TOL_1h.csv). Compatibility between PyPAM and Manata were verified.
